articles.title_orig: World Mission Sunday 2026 | October 18
articles.title_zh: World Mission Sunday 2026 | October 18
articles.content_orig:
About / Offices / Vocations
About / Offices / Vocations
Posted on October 5, 2026 in News
Dear Brothers and Sisters in Christ,
On October 18, we celebrate World Mission Sunday, a powerful reminder of our shared responsibility to proclaim the Gospel to all nations. It is a day when Catholics around the world unite in prayer and solidarity to support the missionary work of the Church.
We are all called to be a part of this mission work. In his last words before ascending to heaven, Jesus told us, “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Mt 28:19), and for 2,000 years the Church has been at work in this task. And we are far from finished! Two-thirds of the people alive — 5.5 out of 8.1 billion — still have no relationship with Christ or his Church. Bringing people to Jesus is the work of the Church, and all of us together have a part to play. Today, we have a singular means to do so: World Mission Sunday.
The second collection we take up on World Mission Sunday helps extend the Church’s missionary work to places where the Church barely exists, where the Gospel has never been heard before, and where the Church is too young, too persecuted, or too poor to sustain herself.
On World Mission Sunday, we stand in solidarity with the missionaries, priests, religious sisters and brothers, and lay leaders serving in the 1,130 mission dioceses — spanning Asia, Africa, Latin America, Oceania, and the Middle East — that depend on our prayers and financial support to continue proclaiming Christ and building His Church.
The year’s World Mission Sunday celebration is unlike any other in our lifetime for two reasons.
First, this World Mission Sunday marks the 100th anniversary of its establishment by Pope Pius XI in 1926. This centenary is an opportunity to mark it with renewed missionary zeal. This year’s theme, “One in Christ, United in Mission,” chosen by Pope Leo XIV, invites us to rediscover the profound unity we share in Christ through baptism and how our baptismal identity overflows into the mission to bring others into communion with God and us.
Secondly, the beatification of Archbishop Fulton Sheen on September 24 reminds us of the importance of the missions. While many know him best for his TV presence, books, and charismatic eloquence, he repeatedly said, “My greatest love has always been for the missions of the Church.” For 16 years, as National Director of The Pontifical Mission Societies in the United States, he poured his talents into World Mission Sunday and distributed the proceeds diligently to the missions. We can surely count on his intercession for World Mission Sunday 2026.
Pope Leo XIV recognizes how important World Mission Sunday is for the Church. He spent a large part of his priestly ministry as a missionary in Peru, serving communities in the Andean highlands and rural villages, and has noted how dependent he was on the support of the Church universal through World Mission Sunday.
Last year, he became the first pope in history to record a short video that could be played before Mass, in which he appealed, “Please help me help missionaries everywhere.” That’s what World Mission Sunday does: to help Pope Leo care for the 1,130 missionary dioceses and territories under his supervision through the Dicastery for Evangelization.
Please respond to his appeal as generously as you can. Visit pontificalmissions.org/wms-2026 for full details.
I am praying that World Mission Sunday will be a blessing for our diocese and help foster increased zeal for the missions within all of us. Let us pray together that the Holy Spirit will renew in us the fire of the early Church, that we might truly be One in Christ, United in Mission, and that we will grow in missionary awareness, solidarity, and responsibility.
In Hope, united in Christ’s mission,
Most Rev. James V. Johnston, Jr. Bishop of Kansas City-St. Joseph

articles.title_orig: Yemeni government forces drive Houthis from Bab el-Mandeb Strait
articles.title_zh: Yemeni government forces drive Houthis from Bab el-Mandeb Strait
articles.content_orig:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have retaken control of the Red Sea port city of Mokha and "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
The Yemeni military said National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces had captured Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes.
Hours earlier, the military said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, but Houthi-run media denied that government forces had made advances in Dhubab.
The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago.
Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive.
Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houth-run Al Masirah TV.
Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences".
The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations".
On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".
It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded.
The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory.
According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east.
A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced.

articles.title_orig: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
articles.title_zh: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
articles.content_orig:
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.
The "very serious incident" happened in the northern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch.
"The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby.
Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days.
There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.
The AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand.
However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl, who was reportedly standing near the teenager, as saying he did not pick up the grenade.
"He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying.
When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified.
"Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media.
A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".
The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said.
Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school.
"At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media.
"Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."
The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on.
"In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."
According to education minister Édouard Geffray, at least 190 students have been injured since the protests began.
Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade.
The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation.
Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".
"His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.
"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."
The recent wave of protests began in late September in Paris and has spread across the country.
High school students started the demonstrations, complaining about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined last week, making similar demands.
More than 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according to AFP, with around 85% of them minors.
The radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a major year of French protest, which saw millions of workers go on strike.
Education minister Geffray said Monday saw a "clear decrease" in the number of schools disrupted compared to recent days, with 589 institutions affected.
Last Friday, French authorities said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been disrupted.
But France is braced for more large protests on Tuesday, as student organisation Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL) has again called on people to take to the streets.
Other organisations, including the teachers' union SNES-FSU, have also shown their support for the students, urging their members to join tomorrow's protest.
In response, the French government said it would set up a "major consultation platform" for students from across the country to share details of the difficulties they have experienced.
Geffray said he hoped to resolve "most of the problematic situations" by 16 October.

Partnership achieves 86% mangrove survival rate in Boca Chica and targets 1,000 planted seedlings by the end of 2026
NORTHAMPTON, MA / ACCESS Newswire / October 5, 2026 / DP World and Fundación Verde Profundo are expanding their mangrove restoration work in Boca Chica after achieving a 86% survival rate among more than 400 seedlings planted in the area's reef lagoon. The partnership now aims to reach 1,000 planted mangrove seedlings by the end of 2026.
Launched in 2025 , the partnership focuses on restoring coastal ecosystems near DP World's Caucedo terminal while strengthening biodiversity and the natural resilience of Boca Chica's coastline. The program includes ongoing monitoring and maintenance to support the long-term growth of restored mangroves.
Monitoring shows that approximately 48% of the planted mangroves have already developed aerial roots, an important sign of growth and adaptation. Mollusks, crustaceans, and juvenile fish have also been observed in restored areas, using the mangroves as shelter and nursery habitat.
The latest restoration activity on September 15 brought together 35 DP World employees and representatives from Fundación Verde Profundo for hands-on conservation work and education about the role mangroves play in protecting marine ecosystems and coastal communities.
"Economic development and environmental protection must advance together," said Manuel Martínez, CEO of DP World in the Dominican Republic . "Our two years of work with Fundación Verde Profundo show how strong partnerships can deliver measurable environmental results. We remain committed to supporting the recovery of coastal ecosystems and helping build healthier, more resilient communities".
Tasha Gough, CEO of Fundación Profundo, highlighted the progress achieved through this collaboration. "Mangrove restoration is a long-term process that requires technical monitoring, continuity, and collaboration among the public, private, and social sectors. One year after the first planting, the high survival rate of the seedlings and their continued development indicate that we are moving in a positive direction. Our goal is not simply to plant mangroves, but to support their establishment and assess how the ecosystem responds over time," she said.
Building a More Sustainable Logistics Hub
The mangrove program forms part of DP World's broader sustainability work in the Dominican Republic. In 2026, the company commissioned a 5,120-kW solar installation expected to reduce CO₂ emissions by more than 3,500 tons annually. DP World is also electrifying its terminal fleet , with now 41 fully electric internal transfer vehicles currently in operation at Caucedo.
The partnership with Fundación Verde Profundo also extends to environmental education. For example, during DP World's Global Volunteer Week , held in connection with the UN's International Volunteer Day, employees, customers, and community partners in the Dominican Republic take part in activities focused on mangrove conservation, biodiversity, and coastal resilience.
Together, these efforts reflect DP World's "Our World, Our Future" sustainability strategy and its approach to reducing the environmental impact of port operations while protecting the ecosystems surrounding them.

articles.title_orig: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.title_zh: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-nine years ago this day, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite to orbit Earth, opening the Space Age and setting off a race with the United States.
Ten years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty came into force.
In 1999, the United Nations started observing World Space Week – from October 4 to 10 – to celebrate the contribution of space technology for the benefit of humanity. Schools, space agencies, museums and astronomy clubs around the world hold stargazing nights, science classes, exhibitions and talks by astronauts and scientists.
Today, more than 80 countries have put satellites into orbit, and people from over 50 of those have travelled to space.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at which countries have done so, how many space travellers have been women, and what comes next for human spaceflight.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet astronaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On board the Vostok 1 spacecraft, he completed one orbit of Earth at about 27,400km/h (17,025mph) during a 108-minute flight. He later ejected from the spacecraft and landed by parachute.
The mission demonstrated that humans could survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry, giving the Soviet Union a major early victory in the Cold War Space Race.
Six years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Signed by the US, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, it established that space should be explored and used peacefully and that no country could claim it as territory.
Less than two years later, NASA’s Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on its surface.
There is no single agreed boundary for where space begins: most international bodies use the Karman line, 100km (62 miles) above Earth, while the US military, NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration count anyone who flies above 80km (50 miles).
Either way, it is closer than it sounds: if Earth were the size of an apple, space would begin about as far from the surface as the thickness of its skin.
By the Karman line measure, at least 746 people from 52 countries have travelled to space, including professional astronauts and paying tourists.
Some hold dual nationality, and some flew for countries that no longer exist, such as the Soviet Union.
The graphic below breaks down space travellers by country.
Two countries still dominate the list. The US has sent 369 people to space, and the Soviet Union and Russia have sent 138 combined. China, the third country to launch people on its own rockets, has sent 29.
Space remains a male-dominated frontier. Science fiction may be full of women commanding starships, but of the 746 people who have travelled to space, only 112, or 15 percent, have been women, about one in seven.
Soviet astronaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to travel to space in June 1963. The US did not follow for another 20 years, until Sally Ride flew in June 1983.
The share of women is rising, though, largely because of commercial flights. More than half of the women who have flown since 2020 went up as paying passengers or guests on Blue Origin’s suborbital rocket.
Most people who have flown to space were in their 30s or 40s on their first flight, which together account for 85 percent. The median age is 40. Commercial flights have widened that range.
The youngest traveller, Oliver Daemen, was 18 when he flew in 2021. The oldest, Ed Dwight, was 90 years and eight months old when he flew in 2024, about two months older than William Shatner had been on his flight three years earlier.
In April 2026, the Artemis II crew flew around the moon and reached about 406,771km (252,756 miles) from Earth, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.
Next is Artemis III in 2027, a rehearsal in Earth orbit to test docking with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. NASA is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts near the moon’s south pole, the first crewed landing since 1972.
India plans its first crewed Gaganyaan flight in 2027, making it the fourth country to launch people on its own rocket. China aims to land astronauts on the moon around 2030.

articles.title_zh: S&P 500 up, Nasdaq at record high as megacap tech stocks rise
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite sailed to a fresh all-time high as traders looked past rising U.S. Treasury yields and digested new economic data.
The Nasdaq Composite was up about 1% and hit an intraday record of $27,478.17. The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded 155 points, or about 0.3% higher. The S&P 500 advanced roughly 0.7%.
Several stocks tied to the artificial intelligence trade led the way higher for the Nasdaq. SpaceX jumped nearly 6%, while hyperscalers Meta and Microsoft ticked up more than 2% and 1%, respectively. Nvidia gained more than 1%, while Tesla rose 2%.
Tech is "sort of like the inverse bond trade," Infrastructure Capital Advisors founder and CEO Jay Hatfield told CNBC. "It's buy tech, sell everything else, and so it's kind of an unstoppable juggernaut."
Hatfield added that tech has served as a kind of safe haven since the pandemic, citing the sector's high earnings-related growth and relatively low sensitivity to interest rates.
"It really doesn't matter what they pay for debt, and the demand for compute is so strong, [so tech is] not really impacted by interest rates," Hatfield said.
As tech stocks rallied, bond yields also advanced. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note  yield was last up more than 6 basis points to 5.341%, while the 30-year was rose about 7 basis points at 5.699%. Both yields surged to multiyear highs in recent weeks, as traders fretted that inflation would lead the Fed to keep rates higher for longer.
Stocks and bonds moved as traders processed the Institute for Supply Management's latest report on economic growth in the services sector. The ISM report showed that the Purchasing Manager's Index grew 54.9% in September, or roughly in line with expectations. However, that figure came in modestly below the index's rate of growth for the previous month.
Investors now turn their attention the Fed, which will release the minutes from its September meeting — potentially shedding light on its decision to hike rates by a quarter of a percentage point last month.
Traders also monitored oil prices, which were lower on Monday. Brent crude futures shed more than 0.7% to trade at $101.51 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude was trading down 1% at $88.53 a barrel.
Stocks are coming off a week defined by surging Treasury yields and a surprisingly lackluster jobs report that helped ease concerns about another Fed rate hike this month. The data provided some relief after a week of pressure from rising bond yields.
"Despite a growing list of headwinds (e.g., geopolitics, higher rates), global equities have climbed c12% YTD and are just below all-time highs," wrote Citi strategist Beata Manthey. "Does this relative calm suggest equity fundamentals will prove resilient to ongoing macro shocks, or will stocks eventually need to correct to more accurately reflect the current risk backdrop? While uncertainty remains high, we still find ourselves in the 'resilience' camp for now."
The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) was up more than 13% in mid-day trading on Monday, pacing for its best day since March 2020.
The ETF's jump comes after the first round results of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, where challenger Flávio Bolsonaro narrowly edged out incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. However, neither received a majority of the vote, and thus will face voters in a runoff election on Oct. 25.
Polls before the first round widely expected Lula to receive the most votes in the initial tally, even though they also showed him trailing Bolsonaro in a potential runoff. Now, following Bolsonaro's overperformance on Sunday, he is seen as the overwhelming favorite to win the runoff.
Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSCM) advanced 2.5% Monday, reaching a 52-week high of $485 per share after Elon Musk suggested his chip venture, Terafab will be partnering with the company for semiconductor factories in Texas.
Musk tweeted a reply post of the report indicating that it was true. Shares of Intel , which had previously said it was partnering with Terafab, are down 4%.
Meanwhile, shares of Musk's SpaceX are up 5.5% after Morgan Stanley said the stock is "cheap and getting cheaper," in a note to clients Sunday. Another catalyst for SpaceX came from Musk proposing a rebrand of its AI unit, from "SpaceXAI" to "SpaceXSI" after President Donald Trump directed the U.S. government to use the term "Super Intelligence" or "SI" instead of artificial intelligence on Sept. 29.
The dollar fell against the Brazilian real on Monday following Sunday's elections in which the Brazilian right was ascendant .
The greenback-to-real exchange rate dropped to 4.99 in Monday morning trading, the lowest level since at least May.
While the presidential contest between incumbent Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, will head to a runoff later this month due to the closeness of the race, senate and governors' races saw wins by conservatives and center-right candidates.
"The result points to gains by the right and the centrão," Brazilian newspaper Folha de S. Paulo reported on Monday .
C.H. Robinson Worldwide announced Monday that it would buy RXO in a stock-and-cash transaction for $5.8 billion. The freight forwarding firm is looking to expand its footprint in North America's truck brokerage business.
While shares of RXO surged more than 20%, C.H. Robinson shares dropped almost 12% in premarket trading.
RXO shareholders would receive $17.25 in cash and 0.0856 C.H. Robinson shares for each RXO share, valuing the company at $30.25 per share, a 29% premium to Friday's close.
The deal values RXO at $30.25 per share, a 29% premium to Friday's close. RXO shareholders will receive $17.25 in cash plus 0.0856 C.H. Robinson shares for each RXO share.
C.H. Robinson CEO Dave Bozeman expects the combination to generate roughly $300 million in annual cost savings within two years of closing.
Bozeman said the deal would allow the company "to create a more scaled, resilient North American third-party logistics provider positioned to offer exceptional customer service and redefine the future of our industry."
The U.S. services sector saw growth in September largely in line with expectations, as both employment and prices saw gains, according to the Institute for Supply Management.
The ISM services index saw a 54.9 reading for the month, down just half a point from August and essentially in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate for 55. The index measures the percentage of purchase managers reporting growth in their businesses.
Within the survey, the employment index rose 2.3 points to 50.1, right over the line indicating expansion. Prices rose 1.4 points to 74, putting the 12-month average at its highest since March 2023. New export orders plunged 9.4 points to 46.9, signaling contraction for the first time in eight months.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded 64 points lower, or 0.1%. The S&P 500 rose marginally along with the Nasdaq Composite .
Shares of Harley-Davidson rose 5.7% Monday after it caught an upgrade from Citi.
The bank upgraded the motorcycle maker to buy from neutral. It also increased its price target on shares to $33 from $31, implying 34% upside from Friday's close of about $24 per share.
Citi analyst James Hardiman said Monday in a note to clients that the motorcycle company is likely to benefit from a major product introduction, cost savings and potential earnings tailwinds from the company's lineup of high performance electric motorcycles called LiveWire.
Bank of America upgraded DraftKings ' rating to buy from neutral on Monday, stating the company's prediction markets are a "win-win" even under regulatory uncertainty.
"While the regulatory future of PMs remains uncertain, we think DKNG is well positioned either way. If PMs stay, DKNG has established itself as the #3 player," said Analyst Julie Hoover. The analyst added they see prediction markets as a "less cannibalization risk."

articles.title_orig: Switzerland becomes first country to ban fur imports and sales
articles.title_zh: Switzerland becomes first country to ban fur imports and sales
articles.content_orig:
In a historic stand against animal cruelty, Switzerland has become the first country in the world to ban both the import and sale of fur.
Last year, the Swiss Federal Council banned all imports of fur and fur products produced using “methods that involve cruelty to animals. ”
Now, the country has taken the next logical step, banning the sale of fur products within its borders, and thus setting a hugely important example for other countries to follow.
As we highlighted last year, we are still waiting on some final details on the exact meaning of “methods that involve cruelty to animals.” What we do know is that this will be decided by the Swiss authorities, not the fur trade, and we strongly encourage them to ensure it includes all sources of fur production.
Given the recent scientific opinion from the European Food Safety Authority and testimony from veterinary associations around the world, anything less than a full ban on products from animals farmed or trapped for their fur would be a travesty.
That’s because there is no way to humanely raise or kill an animal for their fur.
Switzerland’s move should become a watershed moment to end the fur industry once and for all. It is high time for politicians in other countries to follow the lead.
Our team in the United Kingdom recently welcomed the publication of the Government’s Animal Welfare Committee’s opinion on fur sourcing . It made clear the brutal reality of farming and trapping animals for their fur but recognized that more needs to be done at a political level, stating that “consumer and market forces currently do not and cannot provide sufficient pressure to adequately safeguard animal welfare.”
Now the question becomes what can be done to finally put an end to fur.
It’s increasingly recognized that the factory farming of animals for fur is not only immensely cruel and unnecessary—it’s also a danger to public health.
Fur farms pack animals closely together, making these hellish facilities the perfect place for viruses to spread. Because mink are vulnerable to both human and animal influenza viruses, keeping them in large numbers, in cages closely packed together, allows for the spread of COVID and other viruses to humans or other animals living on or near these facilities. In August, the first outbreak of avian flu (H5N1) on a U.S. mink fur farm underscores the urgent reality of these risks.
The cruelty and danger inherent in the fur industry is widely acknowledged. Now we need to harness political will to create permanent change for animals in this space.
This win for animals is also a reflection of just how weak the international fur industry has become. And it is also a testament to the steadfast work of campaigners on the ground there whose persistence has carried the issue forward, through the many legislative steps necessary for this historic outcome.
In this case, the fur trade had recently pushed hard to integrate its own industry-certification scheme into the process. Thankfully, this effort failed, as such scheme would have undoubtably watered down the effectiveness of banning fur imports and sales.
Meanwhile, in the UK, the FurFreeBritain campaign has the support of more than 200 Members of Parliament and Peers and the UK’s new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, recently stated how he was “proud” of the action a previous Labour Government had taken in 2000 to ban fur farming. We urge him to follow Switzerland and move swiftly to introduce a ban on fur imports and sales. Such an initiative that would be as popular and as groundbreaking as that 2000 fur farming legislation. It would end the current double standard that allows the import of fur from animals from other countries who have been caged and killed in fur farms that would be illegal in the UK.
It is time, too, for the European Commission to publish its long-awaited proposal on the future of fur farming and trade in the European Union.
There is no reason for animals to suffer and die for the fur trade. The public knows it, and the calls for an end to the industry are getting louder. The evidence on animal welfare, public health, environmental damage and economic risk grounds is clear: the future must be fur-free.

Tens of millions of animals needlessly suffer and die every year for frivolous fur fashion.
Kitty Block is president and CEO of Humane World for Animals. Follow Kitty Block .

articles.title_orig: ‘Phoenix planet’ may have formed from a dead star’s ashes
articles.title_zh: ‘Phoenix planet’ may have formed from a dead star’s ashes
articles.content_orig:
In a cosmic first, scientists say they have detected a planet that may have formed from the burned remains of its dead host star.
The planet is likely a gas giant orbiting a white dwarf called HS 0209+0832 located about 270 light-years from Earth , according to the authors of a study published Monday in the journal Nature Astronomy. After analyzing observations from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope and other instruments, the team found chemical evidence that suggests the planet could have condensed from material expelled by the star as it fizzled out of energy and collapsed into a white dwarf.
When a sunlike star dies, it first rapidly expands into a red giant and then sheds its outer layers, leaving behind a much smaller but dense, hot core — known as a white dwarf. Some of the first-generation planets, those that originally formed at the same time as the star, can survive this cataclysmic event if their orbit is wide enough. Astronomers have observed a handful of such first-generation survivors revolving around white dwarfs, but never before have they recorded a so-called second-generation planet — an entirely new world made from a dead star’s debris.
Planet found orbiting a dead star could preview what will happen to our solar system
The telltale sign that HS 0209+0832 might have birthed a new planet is unusual traces of heavy elements on the white dwarf’s surface that the study authors believe is planetary material raining down onto the leftover core. “This planetary material is very rich in an element called niobium,” said lead study author Jamie Williams, a doctoral student in the department of physics of the University of Warwick in England. “It’s the first time that this element is found in a white dwarf, and this implies that the planetary material is made from the ashes of the star as it died.”
Further analysis of observations from NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite or TESS revealed a faint brightness signal repeating every 4.4 days — evidence that the researchers say is consistent with a giant planet orbiting the white dwarf.
“What’s interesting about planets orbiting close to white dwarfs is that because white dwarfs cool over time, their habitable zone is very stable. A second-generation planet could form and then be in the habitable zone for tens of billions of years,” Williams said.
Such a large period of stability could provide more ideal conditions for life, but more work is required to validate the second-generation planet discovery, he added. “It’s not a confirmed planet,” Williams said. “It’s only a candidate for now.”
After the red giant phase when a dying star quickly puffs up, it becomes a nuclear furnace that can produce various elements. However, once that fuel runs out and the star transforms into a white dwarf, the heavy elements — including nobium — sink downward rapidly, leaving only lighter elements such as hydrogen and helium on the surface. The researchers determined that the niobium detected on HS 0209+0832 must therefore come from the star’s surroundings. “We think these elements fell onto the white dwarf’s surface because the white dwarf is very hot and emitting loads of extreme ultraviolet radiation, which is stripping the atmosphere of a nearby planet,” Williams said.
The idea of second-generation planets has existed for at least as long as astronomers have known about exoplanets, said study coauthor David J. Wilson, a research associate at the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder.
Scientists detected the very first exoplanets around a pulsar — a type of rapidly rotating dead star — and because pulsars form as a result of massive explosions called supernovas, these planets are likely second-generation, as any original planets would have been destroyed by the immense blast, Wilson explained.
“Although white dwarfs don’t form via supernova, they are surrounded by debris,” he said via email. “You have the planets that were lucky enough to survive the star’s giant phases, the shattered remains of those that weren’t, and leftover gas and dust ejected by the star as it turned from a giant to a white dwarf. So it’s a compelling idea that all that stuff might coalesce into new planets.”
Astronomers still don’t know all the details about how first-generation planets form, which means the potential mechanisms behind this newly reported second-generation planet are even more uncertain. The planet-forming process might have derived from a collision between the dying star and a second celestial body, according to Williams. “There could have been another object close to the core of the star, maybe a star around 20% the mass of the sun, or a brown dwarf,” said Williams, referring to a class of cool objects that are an intermediate between a star and a planet.
If a second object fell into the star during its giant phase, it could have prevented all the dust and gas from spreading out into a massive cloud, making some of it spin in a disk. This disk would then have continued to rotate around the white dwarf, birthing a planet. “In a regular white dwarf there’s no disc, because the star’s material will just be ejected outwards during the red giant phase,” Williams added.
Astronomers discover never-before-seen two-faced star
The researchers plan to use Hubble and NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to observe the system again over the next year, but they also requested time with the more powerful James Webb Space Telescope, which could provide more clues about the existence or features of the planet.
If confirmed, this distant world would belong to an entirely new planetary class and suggest that more second-generation planets could exist around white dwarfs, Williams said.
The discovery would also have implications for our own cosmic neighborhood, Wilson said. “The sun will eventually become a white dwarf, so we’re also looking at the future of the solar system here — maybe the Sun will get a new planet someday!”
The new discovery of a potential second-generation planet is incredibly exciting, said Sarah Casewell, a lecturer at the School of Physics and Astronomy of the University of Leicester, England, who was not involved with the study.
“We know of a large number of white dwarfs that are polluted by planetary material which is similar in composition to rocks within our solar system,” she wrote in an email. “However, in this case, the white dwarf is polluted by incredibly unusual material and the composition of this material is similar to atoms we see being created as stars end their lives.”
More than 95% of all stars in the universe will eventually become white dwarfs, and astronomers have already cataloged hundreds of thousands of them. Finding a planet that has formed after the white dwarf would mean that second-generation planets around other white dwarfs are possible — and that after our sun dies, new planets could emerge in our own solar system, Casewell said.
Radio signal detected for the first time from a planet outside our solar system
Previous observations of white dwarfs have shown that some planetary systems survive a star’s self-destruction, but the recent findings open the possibility of the genesis of new planets, said Amy Bonsor, an associate professor at the University of Cambridge in England, who also did not participate in the work. “This paradigm shift allows us to consider whether in the future we could characterise or investigate the potential habitability of these second-generation planetary systems,” she wrote in an email.
This discovery would also add more evidence to research that has shown planetary systems are varied and complex, even after the host star dies, according to Susan Mullally, a mission scientist at the Space Telescope Science Institute, the science operations center for Hubble.

articles.title_orig: Chiang Mai conference opens to explore “Being Church in the World Today”
articles.title_zh: Chiang Mai conference opens to explore “Being Church in the World Today”
articles.content_orig:
A gathering of World Council of Churches (WCC) commissions and reference groups on Life, Justice and Peace opened in Chiang Mai, where ecumenical leaders will explore what “ Being Church in the World Today” means.
Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, general secretary of the World Council of Churches adressed the Joint Conference of WCC Commissions and Reference Groups on Life, Justice and Peace on the openning day of the conference in Chiang Mai, Thailand, 5 October 2026.
WCC general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, in his opening address, offered a WCC perspective on ecclesiology, mission, witness, and hope.
“ Humanity faces wars and armed conflicts, growing inequalities, displacement and migration, ecological destruction, technological disruption, artificial intelligence, religious and political polarization, declining confidence in institutions, and profound questions concerning human dignity and the future of life itself,” he said. “ At the same time, Christianity itself is experiencing major transformations.”
The church is God's before it is ours, reflected Pillay. “ Here unity is not an ecclesial luxury,” he said. “ It is related directly to Christian witness.”
He further noted that a divided church struggles to proclaim a reconciled Christ. “ This is particularly important for the ecumenical movement,” he said. “ The WCC ’ s understanding of unity cannot be reduced to organizational uniformity.”
Dr Prawate Khid-arn, assistant general secretary for ecumenical relations of the Church of Christ in Thailand, prayed that the meeting will renew people ’ s hearts, deepen their commitment, and give them fresh energy and courage for the journey ahead.
“ May our discussions lead not only to words and recommendations, but also to meaningful actions that bring hope to those who suffer, restore human dignity, strengthen justice, care for God's creation, and contribute to genuine and lasting peace,” said Khid-arn. “ May the Holy Spirit guide your conversations, inspire your discernment, and strengthen our common witness.”
Rev. Grace Moon, general secretary of Christian Conference of Asia, noted the context of the meeting in Asia—a region full of spiritual richness, cultural diversity, and resilience, yet also a place where many still face challenges like inequality, displacement, violence, discrimination, and climate change.
“ Our Christian faith means we cannot ignore suffering or injustice—we are called to stand with those who are hurting, excluded, or silenced,” said Moon. “ We cannot solve these problems alone.”
Moon further noted that climate injustice, conflict, and discrimination are all connected. “ Our calling goes beyond charity—it is about working together for justice, healing, and the well-being of all people and creation,” said Moon.
The conference marks the second time that WCC commissions related to the Life, Justice, and Peace programme are meeting - the first such gathering was held in Geneva in 2024.
The first day of the conference currently underway began with pilgrimage encounters, giving participants an opportunity to meet local communities and organizations in and around Chiang Mai working on issues including clean air, migration, HIV and health justice, and interfaith dialogue.

articles.title_orig: Ebola outbreak shows that the world is not ready for the next pandemic
articles.title_zh: Ebola outbreak shows that the world is not ready for the next pandemic
articles.content_orig:
As Ebola continues to spread in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, the burning question at recent UN pandemic preparedness meetings at the UN General Assembly was: Is the world willing and able to pay for readiness?
When the Marburg virus hit Rwanda in September 2024, the country’s No. 1 goal was stopping community transmission. Marburg, in the same family as the Ebola virus, is second among the top-four deadliest viruses in the world. More than 80 per cent of people who contract the disease die.
The country tracked the source of the zoonotic disease, and using genomic sequencing, sequenced the virus. They discovered that the outbreak was closely related to a sequence that happened in an outbreak of Marburg in Uganda in 2014.
Rwanda mounted an ambitious response by beginning contact tracing, mass testing and surveillance. Ultimately, 9.6 million people were screened by about 54,000 community health workers.
From the diagnosis of the first case of Marburg to the deployment of the first shot of the experimental Sabin Vaccine Institute inoculation was 10 days. The case fatality rate for the outbreak stayed at 22 per cent, the lowest ever recorded for the virus.
Two years on, across the border from Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), has entered Day 139 of its fight against a new strain of an Ebola outbreak, called Bundibugyo. Approximately 3,700 people have died since the outbreak was declared in mid-May 2026. The first encouraging signs of progress to fight it may be emerging.
Rwanda’s response to the Marburg outbreak, hailed the world over, was possible because the country had spent years preparing for such an epidemic. But the DRC is trying to build responses in altogether different conditions: It is coping with a humanitarian crisis amid a war.
So the burning question that dominated the UN’s pandemic preparedness meetings at the General Assembly high-level session last week was: Is the world willing and able to pay for readiness now?
According to the WHO, from 31 August to 20 September, the cases of Ebola in the DRC declined by approximately 26 per cent at the epicenter, Ituri Province. However, in the same period, North Kivu Province, near Ituri, recorded a 73 per cent increase, evidence that the outbreak was evolving across the numerous affected areas.
“Each of the seven affected provinces has its own transmission pattern. One of our greatest concerns is that too many people are still dying before reaching treatment,” said Dr. Marie Roseline Belizaire, the regional emergency director for WHO Africa. She was speaking by Zoom at a recent UN briefing on the Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC and emergency preparedness ahead of El Niño and other health emergencies in the region.
“Every death in the community also increases the risk of further transmission among family members, caregivers, and others involved in burial practices, and although adults account for most confirmed cases,” Dr. Belizaire added. “Children are especially vulnerable.”
On the ground in the DRC, she said that all response teams are working closely with communities to identify suspected cases quickly and to address the misinformation that is keeping people from seeking appropriate care. The bigger emphasis has been moving the response away from major urban centers into rural areas, where the most-worrying epidemiologic trends are occurring.
“The problem is multifaceted,” Dr. Catherine Smallwood, a WHO incident manager for the Ebola response in North Kivu, said in the recent UN event. “There is the access one, and there’s also the issue of funding. We need partners. We need time, we need money, we have a plan, and if we really, truly want to be able to stop this epidemic in the next six months, we will need additional resources.”
For both Rwanda and the DRC, the realities of fighting the Bundibugyo strain are vastly distinct. Rwanda’s health minister, Yvan Butera, spoke at an event during the UN high-level week hosted by the Pandemic Fund, which focuses on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response in low- and middle-income countries, and the governments of Armenia and Rwanda. The forum spotlighted how countries are investing their own resources to close critical preparedness gaps.
Butera said that building a readiness-response plan cannot be done in the middle of a war and humanitarian disaster. The DRC’s effort to control the Ebola outbreak is still lacking an approved vaccine. Provisions of other essential health services are also being carried out under sometimes deadly circumstances.
The services include maternal health, routine immunizations, treatments of malaria and other baseline conditions resulting from widespread displacement of civilians. The decades-long conflict in the eastern DRC involves the M23 militia from Rwanda fighting Congolese troops in competition for the area’s mineral wealth. The violence has made the Ebola outbreak hard to contain.
As of 30 September 2026, data from the Congolese authorities confirmed a total of 3,901 deaths out of 8,067 confirmed cases in the DRC from the outbreak. It has surpassed previous records to become the largest Ebola outbreak in the history of the DRC, but it has not spread to Rwanda. In May 2026, it spread into neighboring Uganda through infected cross-border travelers, but its government halted transmission and was officially declared virus-free by the WHO in August 2026.
Six years ago, the Covid-19 pandemic devastated global health systems, and many countries have yet to fully recover. Mathematical modeling by the Center for Global Development , a nongovernmental organization focused on reducing poverty, suggests that the likelihood of another pandemic of the same scale as Covid within the next 25 years will hit nearly 70 percent. Many global health experts believe the odds are climbing closer to a full certainty.
But the world moves on too quickly, said Wessam Mankoula, the acting head of Emergency Preparedness and Response Division for Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or Africa CDC.
“SARS is over and we forgot, Covid-19 came, we’ve forgotten the devastation,” Mankoula said in a panel on building resilience during last week’s UN General Assembly session. “We need to invest more to build resilient systems now. And to ensure sustainability of our efforts, in the DRC and everywhere else we have to first fight our serious case of pandemic Alzheimer’s.”
Mankoula’s work involves generating resources for the Pandemic Fund to remedy the Ebola outbreak in the DRC. His team is aiming for a fast turnaround of financial pledges into disbursement.
“In the first two months of the response in DRC, we had 10 to 20 per cent success moving from pledges to disbursement,” he said. “The impact was that the first response plan for DRC was $240 million and the second response plan was $1.3 billion. So when there is a delay in dispersing resources, the cost of responding to an emergency dramatically increases.”
According to media reports , $2.9 billion has been raised so far, based on Africa CDC numbers.
Success, Mankoula added, is when the CDC’s support is no longer needed because countries got their pandemic readiness done in “peace time.”
The World Bank operates the Pandemic Fund, whose largest contributors are the US, the European Commission, Germany, Italy and Japan.
“The World Bank and the Pandemic Fund’s priorities are clear. Invest early, invest together, and be ready to act,” Paschal Donohoe, the managing director and chief knowledge officer at the World Bank said at the General Assembly event.
“We learned from the pandemic [Covid-19] that countries that depended on others for the tools that they needed to survive paid a price,” he added.

Quebec City — Technimount EMS (Technimount), a leading provider of mounting solutions for medical devices, is proud to announce that its Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL has been selected as a finalist for the 2026 EMS World Innovation Awards.
Designed specifically for critical care air transport, the Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL transforms a LifePort AeroSled TS stretcher, typically used for adult and pediatric patients, into a neonatal transport system within seconds. The platform securely mounts the Dräger Isolette TI500 incubator while allowing care teams to quickly return the stretcher to standard patient care when neonatal transport is no longer required. By eliminating the need to dedicate a stretcher exclusively to neonatal care, this solution helps air medical teams to optimize equipment utilization while increasing operational flexibility.
At the heart of the system is Technimount’s proprietary XClamp Technology, which remains installed directly onto the stretcher without interfering with its regular use. When neonatal transport is required, the platform can be rapidly installed without tools. A dual quick-release latch system, one securing the platform to the stretcher and the other anchoring the incubator, allows for fast installation and removal. Engineered with the space constraints of aircraft environments in mind, the compact platform remains within the dimensions of the AeroSled TS while providing a secure solution for neonatal transport. The system has been rigorously tested to meet applicable sections of FAA regulations 14 CFR §§ 23 and 25.
The Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL is also designed for seamless compatibility with Technimount’s Xtension Pro Assistant – LP, a previous EMS World Innovation Awards-winning solution. Together, the systems provide teams with the ability to securely manage the incubator and essential medical devices required for neonatal critical care throughout transport.
“Being selected as an EMS World Innovation Awards finalist for a tenth year is an important recognition of the work our team continues to put into solving real challenges faced by critical care transport professionals,” said Carl Bouchard, Founder and CEO of Technimount System. “The Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL was developed to give air medical teams greater flexibility without compromising safety or efficiency, and we are proud to see this innovation recognized by the EMS industry.” Concluded Mr. Bouchard

articles.title_orig: 'What If the World Had 100 More Mother Cabrinis?' Archbishop Golka Visits Mother Cabrini Shrine
articles.title_zh: 'What If the World Had 100 More Mother Cabrinis?' Archbishop Golka Visits Mother Cabrini Shrine
articles.content_orig:
The day before Cabrini Day, Archbishop James Golka made his first official visit to Mother Cabrini Shrine, celebrating a saint whose courage, compassion and missionary faith still challenge Catholics today.
There are certain days at Mother Cabrini Shrine when the past and present seem to come together in a particularly meaningful way. This Cabrini Day is one of them.
As Mother Cabrini Shrine celebrated Colorado’s Frances Xavier Cabrini Day, the Shrine also welcomed Archbishop James Golka for his first official visit — a fitting occasion for the new Archbishop of Denver to visit the holy ground dedicated to a woman whose faith, courage and missionary spirit left such a lasting mark on Colorado.
For Mother Cabrini Shrine, Cabrini Day is much more than a date on the calendar. It is an opportunity to remember the remarkable woman who first came to Denver in 1902 and whose footsteps eventually led her into the foothills west of the city. It was here that Mother Cabrini walked, prayed and cared for the girls from the Queen of Heaven Orphanage. More than a century later, pilgrims continue to come to this same holy ground seeking prayer, peace, healing and a deeper encounter with God.
In 2020, Colorado established Frances Xavier Cabrini Day as a state holiday, observed on the first Monday in October. It became the first paid state holiday in the nation named in honor of a woman — a remarkable distinction and a recognition of the impact Mother Cabrini’s life and work had on Colorado.
But the significance of Cabrini Day extends beyond remembering what Mother Cabrini accomplished more than a century ago. Her life continues to offer an example for the Church and the world today.
Mother Cabrini was a woman of extraordinary faith, but she was also a woman of action. She saw a need and responded. She crossed oceans, overcame obstacles and went wherever she believed God was calling her. Again and again, she said yes — to God, to those who needed her and to the mission placed before her.
(Photo by Jonathan Phillips Photography, courtesy of Mother Cabrini Shrine)
That message was echoed by Archbishop Golka during his homily at the 11:00 a.m. Mass.
Reflecting on Mother Cabrini’s extraordinary life and witness, he said: “If the world had 100 more Mother Cabrinis, the faith and the Church would grow in ways that could hardly be imagined.”
He described Mother Cabrini as a woman who had the heart of a mother, caring deeply for those in need and offering an incredible example of faith lived through service. He also spoke about the importance of seeking the intercession of Mother Cabrini and all the saints, expressing his hope that pilgrims who come to the Shrine experience her intercession in their own lives and emphasizing that her witness remains as important today as it was during her lifetime.
That relevance was especially evident as the archbishop referenced “A Pilgrim People, A Shared Home,” an interfaith letter released in conjunction with Cabrini Day, affirming the dignity of every human life, with particular attention to migrant brothers and sisters. The message carries special significance on a day honoring Mother Cabrini, the patron saint of immigrants, whose ministry was shaped by her determination to accompany immigrants and others who found themselves vulnerable or in need.
More than a century later, the circumstances may be different, but Mother Cabrini’s example continues to call people to recognize the dignity of those around them and to respond with compassion.
After Mass, Mother Cabrini Shrine hosted a Festival of Nations that featured traditional music, dance and food from around the world. (Photos by Jonathan Phillips Photography, courtesy of Mother Cabrini Shrine)
Following Mass, Archbishop Golka greeted the faithful before joining the Shrine community for the Festival of Nations. The celebration was filled with joy and color, with foods representing cultures from around the world, people dressed in traditional clothing, and music and dance, including traditional Matachines dancing.
The celebration of nations is especially fitting on Cabrini Day. Mother Cabrini’s own life crossed borders, cultures and languages, and her mission was rooted in welcoming and caring for people far from home. More than a century later, the many cultures gathered together at the Shrine offered a beautiful reflection of both the universality of the Church and the mission she began.
Archbishop Golka’s first official visit was also a reminder that Mother Cabrini Shrine remains very much alive. Her mission continues through the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, the clergy who serve the Shrine, its staff and volunteers, and the countless pilgrims who make their way to this holy ground each year. The life and ministry of a place like Mother Cabrini Shrine are sustained by many hands, many hearts and a shared commitment to carrying the mission forward.
Cabrini Day offers an opportunity not only to celebrate Mother Cabrini’s extraordinary life, but also to consider what her example asks of all of us today.
Mother Cabrini saw those who were struggling and moved toward them. She trusted deeply in the Heart of Jesus, relied on prayer and refused to let seemingly insurmountable obstacles keep her from the work God had placed before her.
As Archbishop Golka reminded those gathered at the Shrine, the Church still needs Mother Cabrini. And perhaps one of the greatest ways to honor her is to continue the mission she so courageously began.
For those who have never visited Mother Cabrini Shrine — or perhaps have not been in many years — Cabrini Day offers a wonderful invitation to come and discover the woman behind the name. Walk where she walked, pray where she prayed, learn her story and discover why, more than a century later, St. Frances Xavier Cabrini and her mission still have so much to say to the world today.
Colorado Catholic Conference

articles.title_zh: Disease ecologist on the emergence of the new world screwworm and how to stop it
articles.content_orig:
As a new parasite with flesh-eating larvae threatens the nation's livestock industry, a team of Virginia Tech researchers will be on the frontlines of defense.
Led by Luis Escobar, an associate professor of fish and wildlife conservation, the team is working on one of 40 breakthrough projects funded through the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to develop an integrated preparedness and response system against the re-emergence of the new world screwworm in the Americas.
“Preventing a screwworm invasion protects food production, food prices, rural economies, family farms, wildlife populations, companion animals such as dogs and horses, and public health because the screwworms can also affect people,” said Escobar.
Earlier this summer, the USDA confirmed that the new world screwworm fly reached south Texas, threatening the livestock industry for the first time in decades.
Screwworm-related losses exceeded $200 million annually in the 1950s, the equivalent of roughly $1.8 billion today, before eradication efforts succeeded.
According to Escobar, mitigation measures include mandatory physical inspections and anti-parasitic treatments for cattle at southern border ports, as well as stricter movement requirements for animals entering Texas.
As part of the project, Virginia Tech will expand collaborations with Texas A&M, North Carolina State University, the University of Kansas in the United States, Universidad de San Carlos, and Universidad del Valle in Guatemala.
“Rather than addressing one aspect of screwworm control, this project creates a complete decision-support framework that connects surveillance, genetics, producer behavior, and predictive modeling,” Escobar said.
Luis Escobar is an associate professor in the College of Natural Resources and Environment at Virginia Tech. He is a member of the Pandemic Prediction and Prevention Destination Area, the Invasive Species Collaborative, and the Fralin Life Sciences Institute’s Center for Zoonotic and Arthropod- borne Pathogens and Global Change Center.
His research focuses on biogeography, ecology, and evolution of infectious diseases across landscapes.

articles.title_zh: Second QDA Forum Focuses on Real-World Deployments And Progress of Quantum Computing
articles.content_orig:
PRESS RELEASE — The second international Quantum Datacenter Alliance (QDA) Forum highlighted the progress towards commercial deployments and acceleration of distributed quantum computing architectures, while also outlining the next critical areas of focus for progress.
At the iconic Battersea Power Station, London, the QDA brought together technical, business, and government leaders to address one of the most pressing technical and ecosystem challenges: how to integrate emerging quantum hardware into existing and future data center infrastructure.
The agenda explored how quantum systems are moving from lab-scale demonstrations toward commercial deployment, highlighting that system level architecture, control, error correction, interoperability and power consumption have become as critical as the qubits themselves. Attendees also emphasised the importance of open sharing, interoperability, and collective thinking about the direction and future uses of quantum technologies.
Dr. Carmen Palacios-Berraquero, Founder and CEO of Nu Quantum said, “As quantum computing moves towards large-scale utility, collaboration becomes critical. The QDA brings the industry together to tackle the shared challenges of building quantum computing as infrastructure — scalable, interoperable, reliable and efficient — and ultimately making quantum compute accessible to the world, responsibly.”
Dame Wendy Hall, speaking about lessons from classical computing and AI,said, “It’s all about communication. It is so important to get the positive messages out about any new technology ahead of the inevitable scare stories about the risks and potential harms which the media love to pick up on. Of all the new technologies on the horizon though. Quantum computing is the hardest to explain to non technical audiences. That messaging will need a lot of work as the technology begins to emerge into the public arena.”
Hannah Boardman, Director responsible for AI, Quantum, Engineering Biology, Semiconductors, Robotics, Department for Science, Innovation & Technology , said, “Initiatives like this QDA show the power of bringing together different sections of the ecosystem across technologies, thinking in a different kind of way and focusing on delivering common goals to be identified in the room.”
Petrina Anne Steele, Head of Emerging Technologies at Equinix , said, “Quantum is an incubating technology that sits alongside classical HPC and now AI environments, and is highly complementary. Hybrid infrastructure is making quantum commercially actionable today. We already have companies doing high precision molecular modelling and exploring FX trading optimisation.”
Ben Bloom, Founder and CEO at Atom Computing , said, “Over the past two days, Nu Quantum and its partners have been exploring how to integrate quantum systems into a data center. This is an incredibly important topic as we continue to expand the reach of quantum computers to more and more industries and more and more users. Building a utility scale quantum computer doesn’t just fall to one company, and doesn’t even just fall to one technology. It’s the combination of multiple components together that will actually bring out a utility scale quantum computer.”
Looking ahead, the QDA will continue to convene industry leaders through future forums, working groups, and events, driving the industry toward scalable, robust, commercially viable quantum computing.

articles.title_orig: U.S. officials seeking details of reported Russian plague death, quarantines
articles.title_zh: U.S. officials seeking details of reported Russian plague death, quarantines
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of people were reported to be in isolation after a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague and other infectious diseases died of an undisclosed illness.
The researcher, a 28-year-old female laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia, in the town of Shelekhov, died after being diagnosed with a pneumonia of “unknown” origin, according to Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that handles infectious disease.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the administration was watching the situation closely .
“I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it,” Rubio said.
Rospotrebnadzor has played down the link between the death of the researcher — named in local media as Darya Shipilova — and her work.
“No micro-organisms associated with the employee’s professional duties were detected in samples taken from the patient,” it asserted, adding that the “epidemiological situation” in the region was stable.
Nevertheless, the agency’s head, Anna Popova, traveled to Irkutsk on Friday, according to the local governor, Igor Kobzev, for what he described as an extraordinary meeting of the regional anti-epidemic commission.
The meeting was in connection with a “suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection affecting a resident of the region,” Kobzev said on Telegram.
Reached by phone on Monday, the institute where the researcher worked told CNN it was not commenting on the incident .
Regional authorities are implementing a “comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures,” according to Maxim Modin, the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district in eastern Russia, near the Mongolian border.
The inpatient facility at the hospital where the worker was treated has been placed under quarantine, and several departments have stopped discharging or admitting patients, Modin said. Other hospitals in the region have also been closed, according to local media reports.
Irkutsk authorities also cancelled the annual community clean-up event that was scheduled for the weekend — a decision local media linked to the incident.
The woman’s death was confirmed by officials last week.
Ekaterina, a resident of Shekelov, told CNN on Monday that there were no visible changes in the city, but locals were anxious. “My acquaintances are slightly panicking,” she said.
Another resident, who wished to remain anonymous, said he was “shocked” by the news.
Unofficial reports, including by the independent regional news outlet Liudi Baikala, have said that nearly 200 people are under observation.
There have been no cases of infectious diseases reported among institute staff over the past 10 days, and all of the employee’s recent contacts are being tested and examined, Modin said.
In its only comment on the incident, the Kremlin said people should only trust updates coming from the official agency.
“One should rely on official statements from Rospotrebnadzor rather than listening to various rumors and speculation,”  Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday.
The World Health Organization told CNN it was in contact with the Russian health authorities to “verify the event, its circumstances, the laboratory tests underway, and their results.”
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” it said.
Despite such reassurances, several countries in the region have put in place safeguarding measures.
Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Health said that while the risk was “very low”, the situation was being monitored and “sanitary and quarantine controls were implemented at state border crossing points.”
Uzbekistan said it “increased the readiness” of relevant authorities to deal with highly infectious diseases. Kyrgyzstan, which does not share a land border with Russia is some 1,500 miles from Irkutsk, announced Monday it was introducing quarantine controls at state border crossing points.
A virologist in Siberia, Alexander Chepurnov, told CNN that the strict protocols being followed were designed to prevent onward spread.
“After any suspected exposure, staff are instructed to immediately report it, decontaminate, undergo medical assessment and be isolated in a separate dedicated facility for however long they might be infectious,” Chepirnov said.
Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Organization, told CNN that while pneumonic plague is deadly, it is not very transmissible and one would have to be exposed to a high bacterial load to become sick.
In that sense, it is unlike respiratory illnesses such as COVID, she said.
There is endemic plague among wildlife in parts of Siberia, Rassmussen added.
According to its website, the Anti-Plague Institute employs around 95 researchers and is a major public health facility responsible for monitoring and preventing outbreaks of high-risk bacterial and viral infections across Siberia and Russia’s Far East.
The head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, said earlier that the employee died “possibly from the plague,” but noted there had been no outbreak of the disease in his region.
Pneumonic plague is one of three types of plagues that are caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
The other two types typically spread from contact with infected fleas, animals or infected tissues.
An aluminum plant near the laboratory instructed staff to wear masks as a precautionary measure. The director of Irkutsk Aluminum Plant, Artem Fominikh, noted “conflicting reports” were circulating and called for calm.
Oldest known evidence of plague reveals the disease’s deadly impact 5,500 years ago
The infection in the Irkutsk region is “most likely not the plague, but even if confirmed, there will be no spread of this disease,” a former head of Rospotrebnadzor, Gennady Onishchenko, said on Friday.
Onishchenko told state news agency TASS that the onset of cold weather would likely prevent transmission.
A US State Department spokesperson told CNN Sunday that it was aware of the possible death due to pneumonic plague in Russia.
“We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” the spokesperson said. “Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.”
Patients with pneumonic plague develop fever, headache, weakness and and “a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucous,” according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The World Health Organization notes that the plague has a high fatality rate, but is also easily treated with antibiotics if caught early.
