articles.title_orig: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.title_zh: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.content_orig:
After a volcano erupted on tiny Tristan da Cunha in the South Atlantic, the 264 displaced islanders told the BBC about their first taste of modern British life.
"Just over a year ago, they'd never seen traffic or a road or a house higher than a cottage," said Tim Brinton in a 1963 BBC programme. He was talking about the residents of Tristan da Cunha, the world's most remote inhabited island. In the middle of the South Atlantic Ocean, roughly halfway between Cape Town in South Africa and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, the tiny British outpost is more than 1,500 miles from any other populated land, and is only accessible by a seven-day boat journey.
But on 10 October 1961, a sudden volcanic eruption blasted the islanders out of their splendid isolation and into the industrialised modern world. "We heard the rumbles first, then the ground just automatically cracked… Then the smoke and the fire started coming out the ground," one of them told the BBC in a 1998 film. Another, Mary Swain, said that she'd run to her husband and shouted, "Jump up quick, Fred, the Earth is opening!"
The island's volcano had been dormant since Tristan was first settled 150 years earlier. But great cracks appeared in the ground a few hundred metres from the main village, which is named Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. By the time the islanders had escaped in their fishing boats to nearby Nightingale Island, their homes were already threatened by lava. "The whole place is vibrating with earthquakes," announced a BBC reporter, "and the eastern corner is cracking and breaking up."
Tristan's 264 inhabitants were forced to evacuate , picked up by a Dutch liner that happened to arrive the next day. Within hours, the whole community was aboard, leaving everything apart from the few things they could carry with them – "a rifle, an overcoat and a lamp," recalled Swain – and their boats, which they stored in their gardens when they reached England weeks later.
They were housed on a disused military airbase near Southampton, a port city on England's south coast. "So much is strange to them," said Brinton. "They'd never seen shops because on the island, money wasn't used. Boats were their livelihood. For them, there's been no industrial revolution. And for 150 years, they've lived simple agricultural lives out of touch with world progress."
Though Tristan da Cunha was discovered in 1506 by a Portuguese admiral who gave it his name, it was another 300 years before it supported anything but seabirds and seals. The UK annexed the island in 1816 to prevent it being used as a base for attempts to free Napoleon Bonaparte from his imprisonment on the South Atlantic island of St Helena . The following year, a Scotsman, Corporal William Glass, stayed behind when the British garrison was withdrawn. With his family and a few others, he founded the first permanent community.
In History is a series which uses the BBC's unique audio and video archive to explore historical events that still resonate today. Sign up to the accompanying weekly newsletter.
By 1961, the population of the 40 sq miles (100 sq km) of volcanic rock had risen to 264, many of them survivors from ships wrecked on the island, with just seven family names between them. On several occasions, the failure of the potato crop or the wrecking of fishing boats brought the islanders to the point of starvation. But they stayed on, even defying several attempts by the British government to evacuate them.
When the volcanic eruption forced the islanders to leave, they faced difficulties settling in England. They had never seen a car, a bicycle, a TV set or an income tax form. And it was a challenging climate. "Here is too much gas and smoke," Tristanian Joey Repetto told the BBC in 1963. On his journey to their initial accommodation, he said, "I steady coughed without stopping."
Adapting to the nine-to-five work pattern also proved tricky for the community of farmers and fishermen. "Here, when you go to work in the morning, you've got one job. You've got to look forward all the whole week of getting up at the same time, going to the same place, doing the same work every day," said Joey's father Gerald, who was used to a more varied life determined by natural rhythms.
Similarly, financial pressures placed new demands on the islanders, as Swain explained. "In England, you need money for your living. But on Tristan, we don't. If we haven't got no money, well, we just go without it. It don't bother us at all… if I've got no money, I still can go out and get my own potatoes. I can still go and get my own fish."
She didn't hold back on expressing her views on British life. "We don't like the weather... There's too much sickness and we don't like the place at all."

Despite having a single policeman on the island, who wore a British uniform, Tristan had almost no crime. The community was shocked by an incident in England when one member was attacked and hurt by two youths, who took his most valued possession, a gold watch, and smashed it.
But there were some elements of British life that were appreciated by the Tristanians, particularly the younger ones, who described a love of Italian suits and record players. "Country and western music is our favourite, by Johnny Cash and Ernest Tubb," said one teenager, who also enjoyed the social dances. "Since I come here, I've been doing the twist and the locomotion, all that lot. We've forgotten how to do the waltz. But I like to twist myself."
Despite that, most of the islanders were keen to return home. In 1962, the British government sent a survey party to study conditions on Tristan. While the volcano was still smoking, the geologists judged that it was now dormant.
Surprisingly little damage had been done to the village of Edinburgh. The lava had turned at the last moment and flowed into the sea, something that the islanders considered to be an act of God. Some of the thatched roofs were burnt, but the cottages were mostly intact. Yet in their absence, houses had been ransacked and some livestock stolen by passing sailors.
Many animals were still alive, however, with the chickens multiplying in number. Though the dogs had run wild and slaughtered the sheep, the cattle had kept themselves well-fed on the lush island grass, and there were new calves. Lava had covered the beaches, but return was possible.
The British authorities held a secret ballot in the community hall at the islanders' RAF camp. All Tristanians over the age of 21 voted, and the result was an almost unanimous vote to return, 148 to five in favour. After an advance party went back to plant seeds for the following year's potato crop, most of the islanders arrived at Tristan da Cunha in November 1963.
When asked what she was most looking forward to on the island when she returned, Swain told the BBC: "A free life. We can get our own fish and everything of our own back there without money."
Elaine Repetto, who was born on the island but chose to leave in 1984, told the BBC in 1998 why it held such a pull. "We are strongly independent and used to battling with the elements in order to survive… We have to rely upon each other in a way you would find in few other places."
She described the impact of the events in 1961. "Today, the volcano is still a smoking reminder of the events which shaped our view of ourselves and our contact with the outside world."

articles.title_orig: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.title_zh: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.content_orig:
UCSF’s $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital is scheduled to open in 2030, but it wont’t fix the university’s staffing crisis, write Drs. Akshar Rambachan and Anand Habib.
Every day, we watch our patients and fellow physicians pay the price for a strained system we didn’t build and can’t fix alone.
We are doctors at UCSF. At UCSF’s flagship Parnassus Hospital, people sick enough to need a hospital room wait on gurneys in emergency-room hallways because there aren’t enough staffed hospital beds.
We see patients attached to IV antibiotics laying on beds outside ER bathrooms. Elderly patients with hip fractures and pain languish under bright lights and constant noise until, deprived of sleep, they develop delirium. Families are forced to discuss end-of-life wishes within earshot of strangers in the hallway.
These are the daily realities at what should be a world-class health-care system. It’s a patient-care crisis driven by a dysfunctional system that we, as doctors, had no hand in building — or get a say in changing.
For generations, doctors had the authority and independence to make structural staffing choices to deliver high-quality patient care. Physicians owned practices, allowing them to control their patient load and shape the staffing team.
That world is disappearing. Physicians increasingly work as employees of sprawling health systems in which decisions about staffing, workload, compensation and budgets are made further and further from the bedside.
Whatever the administrators are doing clearly isn’t working. UCSF’s emergency wait time is more than 20% higher than the national average .
When UCSF patients are finally seen, their average length of patient stay is 60% higher than the state average — which strongly correlates with negative patient outcomes .
The Parnassus ER has more than double the national average of patients who leave without seeing doctors.
As doctors, we write emails, join committees, conduct studies and share proposals shaped by our years of training, research and experience to address this crisis. Our reports, requests, complaints and proposals are treated as suggestions and all but ignored.
That is why we and physicians across the University of California system are organizing a union.
The mayor and allied organizations say a ballot measure to spend $120 million on housing would create a ‘slush fund,’ but its advocates deny the charge
The number of new cases decreased last year by 8%, but community members are worried as changes to federal safety nets such as Medicaid take effect
Team supporters are celebrating the second playoff berth in as many seasons, creating game-day atmospheres that mirroring ‘Ballhalla’
UCSF’s solution to the patient care crisis is the $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital, scheduled to open in 2030. Let us be clear — we support the new hospital. Parnassus needs more critical inpatient and emergency rooms, and our patients deserve modern facilities.
But fancy new buildings don’t treat patients — people do. The expansion can’t be a substitute for solving the real crisis: the decreased investment in frontline staffing, resulting in chronic shortages that make it impossible to provide patients with world-class care.
We are often told that capital spending and staffing come from different budgetary “pots.” The accounting may separate capital and operating expenses, but the underlying finances are interconnected. UC’s own debt policy makes that clear: Medical centers seeking external financing must demonstrate adequate operating income, cash on hand and the ability to cover their debt payments .
In other words, financing what UCSF builds for tomorrow depends on the operating performance of the health system today — which is to say, on the people doing the work.
You cannot grow a system by hollowing out the front-line workers who make it run. Commitments to adequate staffing, sustainable workloads, and retention of the people required to operate new hospitals should not be revisited every budget cycle, revocable with every change in leadership. They should be codified and fixed to maintain continuity and quality.
To deliver on our mission to do everything in our power to get the best outcomes for our patients, doctors need a say not only in how we provide care, but also in the conditions within which that care happens.
We need mechanisms to ensure sufficient staffing at all levels, guardrails on how technology is used in patient care, and safe worksites that support healthy outcomes for our patients — not wait times that cause suffering and worsen their symptoms.
Through the UC Physicians Committee, doctors across specialties and campuses are organizing with University Professional and Technical Employees union, alongside many of the pharmacists, therapists and other professionals we already work with every day.
Together, we can codify common-sense policies so that every part of a patient’s care team is set up for success.
The Helen Diller Hospital is a promise about what UCSF intends to be in 2030. The medical professionals caring for San Franciscans today deserve a binding voice in what it is now. A union is how we get one, so that the institution we’re proud to work for can be the one that its patients were promised.
Dr. Akshar Rambachan is a hospital-medicine physician at UCSF. Dr. Anand Habib is an internal-medicine physician at UCSF.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico that people should accept the risks of AI in order to gain its benefits. “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” he told the site. The trade-off will be worth it, he argued: “I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ‘We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen’ … Because I think people will do tremendously—orders of magnitude more—good stuff than bad stuff.”
That’s a tone shift from Altman. When he talked to Fortune’s Alyson Shontell recently , he was more cautious. A 10% risk of AI killing us all by the end of the decade is unacceptable, Altman said. He insisted that OpenAI has not, and would not, take that risk.
“We are entering a new era,” he said. “We are clearly, today, at a point on the curve with great potential and real risk.”
“We have not solved alignment,” he said, referring to efforts to create AI that’s aligned with human values. “I believe no lab has solved alignment. I get nervous when I hear rumors that people think they sufficiently solved alignment, that they can continue training and it’s okay because their model is a nice guy and isn’t going to do anything wrong.”

The global fertility rate for humans has never been lower, according to a recent deep-dive into global demographics from Moody's Ratings.
“The global fertility rate has declined from 4.9 children per woman in 1950 to around 2.2 today, only slightly above the replacement rate of 2.1,” the team there said. “More than 70% of the world's population now lives in countries with fertility rates at or below replacement level.” In Singapore, the government takes the problem so seriously it has started its own dating service for public employees .
The problem is that birth-rate shrinkage is a compounding problem, Moody’s says: “A fertility rate of 1.0 produces a generation roughly half the size of the one before it. At 0.8, population decline compounds even more rapidly. These effects take decades to emerge but are difficult to reverse.”

articles.title_zh: Chester County has more measles cases than most entire states in the country
articles.content_orig:
Nine out of 10 unvaccinated individuals who come in contact with measles will get sick.
In late June, Chester County reported two cases of measles, as an outbreak in bordering Lancaster County crossed into the farmlands that blend into the suburban sprawl of Philadelphia’s collar communities.
Case numbers grew tenfold in July, and by late August, three dozen people had gotten sick up and down the county’s western border.
The latest numbers now show 83 measles cases in Chester County , more than most entire states have seen all year, making it a locus in Pennsylvania’s largest measles outbreak in more than three decades.
Chester is the first county in the Philadelphia region to grapple with wide circulation of a highly contagious virus that could spread like wildfire if it reaches other under-vaccinated communities, especially densely populated ones closer to the city.
As cases rise in Chester County, public health officials are ramping up educational outreach, scheduling pop-up clinics, and even bringing doses of the vaccine to people’s homes, all in an effort to contain known hot spots in the outbreak.
At Chester County’s schools, homecoming parades, and grocery stores, many families say they are aware of the outbreak, but are not deeply concerned. Those who are vaccinated worry more that their social and school lives may be disrupted, as they were during the COVID-19 pandemic, if the virus continues to spread.
Anne Nemeth, who lives in Paradise in Lancaster County, feels only a little worried, given that her two sons are vaccinated.
At a time of declining vaccination rates , she isn’t sure whether some of her closest neighbors, who the family regularly gets together with, are vaccinated.
They are Amish, and she has read that many of the people getting sick in her area were part of the Plain community. Two Amish infants in Lancaster County died in August after contracting measles in the state’s first deaths linked to the outbreak.
“I’m hoping they would tell us if they were sick,” she said. “It’s a lot of trust.”
Pennsylvania has reported five deaths associated with measles. A 20-year-old Amish woman who died lived just over the Chester border in Lancaster County. She wanted the vaccine after her parents and eight siblings got sick, but couldn’t get it because she was being treated for leukemia.
Close to 1,000 people statewide have been sickened by the virus, marking one of the most robust outbreaks the United States has seen in years. And experts say the cases that have been reported are likely an undercount, as many people do not seek medical care for their symptoms and some have been reluctant to speak with the health department.
“Public health is now in a race with the disease,” said Dale Weiser, the clinical services supervisor for Chester County’s health department. “It’s going to either burn through all the susceptible people, or we’re going to make fewer people susceptible through vaccination. That’s the only way it ends.”
Measles is so contagious that nine out of 10 unvaccinated individuals who come in contact with the disease will get sick.
That’s how a county like Chester, with one of the highest vaccination rates in the state, has also come to log the third-most cases in the outbreak.
Chester County’s kindergarten measles vaccination rate falls just below the 95% threshold that scientists say is necessary to keep the virus from spreading widely. Kindergarten vaccination offers a view into a community’s protection because the vaccines are required for school attendance.
But the county — like the rest of the Philadelphia region — is pockmarked with areas where vaccination has dropped well below the so-called herd immunity threshold, leaving families vulnerable to severe illness.
In eastern Chester County, for instance, five elementary schools in West Chester had kindergarten measles vaccination rates below 95% — one of the vulnerable areas in the region identified by an Inquirer analysis of 2025-26 school-level data.
Farther east, Chester City in Delaware County , and neighborhoods in West and North Philadelphia have also similarly seen measles vaccination rates drop below so-called herd immunity.
In Chester County, the health department seeks to limit the virus from spreading from west to east across the county, where it would reach more densely populated communities, said Jeanne Franklin, Chester County’s health director.
“If it finds that pocket of unvaccinated individuals, it’s going to popcorn until it finds no one left,” Franklin said.
The health department began reaching out to hospitals and schools months before Chester County reported its first cases, because public health leaders knew it was likely only a matter of time before the virus spread from Lancaster County, Franklin said.
Hospitals were asked to develop a measles screening protocol, if they didn’t have it already, so that early symptoms, such as fever, cough, and runny nose, wouldn’t be dismissed as seasonal illnesses.
Schools were urged to start tracking vaccine status among staff. When a school identifies a measles case, the county requires any student or staff member who is unvaccinated or does not have proof of vaccination to stay home for 21 days, Franklin said. Since many adults don’t have their vaccination records handy, that could create a major staffing disruption.
As case counts in Chester County grow, pop-up vaccine clinics have been scheduled across the county.
The health department has administered more than 500 doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine so far this year, most of them since the outbreak began in April.
The health department’s nurses will bring doses of the vaccine to homes and farms of residents who don’t travel. Vaccines are also available at the county’s health clinics.
Many of the parents lined up along Atglen’s Main Street last week for the local school district’s homecoming parade said they did not feel a reason to be deeply concerned about the outbreak because their families are vaccinated.
“I guess I have the same level of concern as I have for all sickness with kids in public schools,” said Sandi Wrigley, a Cochranville mother whose children, ages 9 and 11, are vaccinated. “If we take the time to worry about that, it’ll be an endless worry.”
Until recently, measles was considered eradicated in the United States, and despite declining vaccination rates, most families are still choosing to vaccinate their children.
Some were angry that measles is even a conversation.
Michael Lavender, from Parkesburg, said vaccinating his 12-year-old daughter was an “easy decision.”
“I really feel like there should be no reason to even talk about it,” he said.
On the other side of the county, families lined up inside the Great Valley Middle School gymnasium in Malvern for flu and COVID-19 vaccines.
Kevin Wrabley, of Malvern, doesn’t worry about his 11-year-old son contracting measles because he is vaccinated. But he does worry about other children and adults who aren’t able to get vaccinated.
“It’s discouraging, things we thought were safely behind us are coming back,” he said.
In Chester County, public health educators have the task of trying to untangle the myriad reasons people are opting out of a vaccination. Many have little to do with science: Two doses of the measles vaccine provide 97% protection — better than most vaccines.
The MMR vaccine is among those long required to attend school in Pennsylvania and every other state. But families here have increasingly been deciding against vaccination for religious and philosophical reasons, as state law permits, often by simply printing and signing a form noting their objection.
Some fluctuations in kindergarten vaccination rates are typical from year to year, but the rise of anti-vaccine rhetoric in federal leadership and a growing distrust in public health authorities has exacerbated fears about vaccination.

articles.title_orig: The 10 Senate seats most likely to flip in 2026
articles.title_zh: The 10 Senate seats most likely to flip in 2026
articles.content_orig:
Nearly four weeks out from Election Day, the Senate battleground map is growing after signs of improvement for Democrats in several red-leaning states.
For the first time this year, CNN’s list of 9 Senate seats most likely to flip expands to 10 to include Kansas, which hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years . A new wave of polling also shows Democrats ahead or competitive in red states like Ohio, Alaska and Texas. All four states went for President Donald Trump by double digits in 2024.
To win the Senate majority, Democrats will need to pick up four Republican-held seats while defending three of their own, including Michigan.
Trump’s approval rating stands at 34%, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls, amid high frustration over the economy and the war he launched against Iran. Democrats have also seen surging enthusiasm in special elections since Trump returned to office and early signs of elevated turnout in early voting.
But they have also expressed unease over the massive amount of spending coming from the GOP. From the start of October through Election Day, Republicans are poised to outspend Democrats on advertising in eight of the ten most competitive Senate races, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact, even though that advantage will be blunted by GOP-aligned outside groups having to spend more for ratings points than Democratic campaigns will.
Our ranking of the seats most likely to flip in November is based on CNN reporting, including conversations with strategists involved in Senate races, as well as our analysis of candidate fundraising, polling and the partisan environment in the states. The rankings are a snapshot of where the contests stand at this point and can shift as the midterm election season enters its final month.
North Carolina remains the state most likely to flip this year. Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper, who has made affordability issues a centerpiece of his campaign, has a strong position over GOP nominee Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman and Trump ally vying to replace Sen. Thom Tillis.
An Elon University/YouGov poll released last month showed Cooper up 11 points over Whatley among likely voters. The Senate Leadership Fund, a key Republican outside spending group, is pausing its ad campaign there. Over the weekend, Republican outside groups cut more than $15 million from their remaining ad bookings, according to AdImpact data.
Still, Trump campaigned with Whatley in North Carolina last month in an effort to turn out his base in a state he won three times.
Ohio moves up two spots on this list, a reflection of the prime position of former Sen. Sherrod Brown.
Brown, who lost reelection to a fourth term by less than four points two years ago, has led GOP Sen. Jon Husted in most polls. A New York Times/Siena University poll of likely voters conducted at the end of September showed a tight race, Brown at 49% and Husted at 46%, within the survey’s margin of error. A Marist poll of registered voters in Ohio showed Brown up eight points over Husted last month.
In the NYT/Siena University poll, Husted’s favorability is at 37% while Brown is at 46%. That’s perhaps a reflection of Brown having a longer history with many Ohio voters than Husted, the former lieutenant governor appointed to take Vice President JD Vance’s seat last year.
Brown’s attacks on Husted over data centers – calling him “the face of data centers in Ohio” – have proven particularly potent as Republicans’ campaign arm in Washington has warned the issue is an “anchor” on Husted’s campaign.
Senate Democrats last week blocked a Husted-sponsored bill that would have recommended states take action on data center-related energy costs. And campaigning for Husted on Saturday, Trump defended data centers in southwestern Ohio, a reflection of the president’s longstanding opposition to pausing their construction.
In one buzzy digital spot released last week, Brown’s campaign also featured voters using expletives as they reacted to Husted’s past comments suggesting people living in poverty are “not very experienced at navigating the real world.” (Brown’s campaign is running an expletive-free version of the ad on TV.)
Republicans have pulled from a 2024 playbook to run ads attacking Brown on transgender politics, hoping that will move the needle in the state. Brown has responded with a TV spot of his own featuring voters talking about how Ohio already has laws addressing transgender policies and wanting candidates to focus on other issues.
One big question heading into the final stretch is whether GOP spending could help tighten this race. Republican groups are set to spend more than $80 million there from the start of October through Election Day while Democrats have allotted more than $50 million.
Alaska moves up two spots. The enormous and sparsely populated state is notoriously hard to poll, but a NYT/Siena poll of likely voters released Saturday found Democrat Mary Peltola up seven points over GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, 50 to 43%.
November’s contest will be determined by ranked-choice voting, and two others join Sen. Sullivan and Peltola on the ballot, including another GOP candidate named Dan Sullivan, a former schoolteacher. The possibility of voters confusing the same-name candidates has been a point of concern for Republicans ahead of November.
Democrats consider Peltola, a former congresswoman, as one of their strongest recruits, and she’s kept some national Democratic politicians like former Vice President Kamala Harris at arm’s length at a time when her opponent attempts to tie to her to “lower-48 liberals.”
Sullivan stood beside Trump in the Oval Office to tout a $54 billion investment from South Korea for the Alaska LNG pipeline project just weeks before the election. Peltola also moved quickly to praise the president’s announcement, saying she looks forward to “continuing this bipartisan work” with Trump.
Peltola’s demeanor towards aides and use of vulgar rhetoric came under scrutiny last month with a New York Times report detailing allegations of hostile behavior from some former aides. Her campaign denied any pattern of abusive pattern but acknowledged that Peltola has struggled at times to deal with the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023. Alaska’s other Republican senator, Sen. Lisa Murkowski, also came to her defense , noting Peltola’s personal struggles.
Maine drops two spots on our list. But the race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson remains extremely competitive as the two prepare to debate for the first time this week.
A University of New Hampshire poll conducted last month found Jackson slightly ahead of Collins among Maine likely voters – 51% to 47% - marking the first public survey showing the Democrat with the advantage in the state. Other recent polls, including a CNN survey conducted by SSRS and a NYT/Siena poll , have shown no clear leader.
Collins remains in a vulnerable position given Harris won her state by 7 points in 2024. Polling has indicated the contest hinges more on negative views of the Maine senator and Trump than it does on perceptions about her Democratic opponent.
Democrats have hammered Collins for siding with Trump on consequential votes even as she’s struck out on her own on issues like tariffs and the Iran war. They have also seized on a ProPublica report alleging Collins’ office was involved in a pay-to-play scheme during her 2020 campaign. Collins has forcefully denied the allegations as a “political hit job.”
Collins has survived tough reelection battles in the past, and Republicans are leaning hard on reminding constituents of what she’s accomplished for the state. GOP groups also have spent millions on corruption ads of their own against Jackson, a former Maine Senate president, along with TV spots hammering the Democrat on tax policy .
Starting Tuesday, Collins and Jackson will have four debates over ten days.

articles.title_zh: What Would You Do If Your Employer Could Destroy the World?
articles.content_orig:
On September 8, Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old Anthropic employee, posted a resignation statement on X that ricocheted around the internet. Coxon was a capabilities researcher, meaning he worked to make models more powerful and autonomous. He quit in protest of what he saw as the company’s suicidally reckless pursuit of artificial general intelligence.
To the AI community, an Anthropic employee believing that their company’s technology might end the world is not exactly news. (Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI employees who believed OpenAI, if left unchecked, would do just that.) But an Anthropic employee publicly quitting in protest is. OpenAI and Anthropic are among the most powerful companies in the world. They work at the cutting edge of their field, building what most of them believe to be the most important technology ever to exist. When someone leaves one lab, they often go straight to its rival. Daniel Kokotajlo, who resigned from OpenAI in 2024, recalls a researcher telling him that quitting a lab was akin to “renouncing your citizenship. Now you’re a nobody. Who is going to protect you?”
A debate soon broke out: If you’re a lab employee who believes in these risks, what should you do? Is it best to leave in defiance? Or is it better to agitate from the inside, close to the seat of power? And how would the choice affect your friendships and community?
Coxon was joining a small set of employees of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind who, over the years, chose to walk away. New York Magazine, in collaboration with Asterisk magazine, brought together eight of them. The members of this group left for different reasons. A few, like Coxon and Kokotajlo, wanted to call attention to the risks of accelerating AI progress. Others objected to their employers’ partnership with the Department of Defense or felt frustrated as what had once been an idealistic nonprofit turned into a corporate juggernaut. And some simply felt that their work — whether it was on safety or widespread job loss — would be more valuable on the outside.
Miles Brundage, OpenAI, 2018–24, head of policy research Rosie Campbell, OpenAI, 2021-24, policy-frontiers team lead Jacob Coxon, OpenAI, 2023–26, Anthropic, May–September 2026, capabilities researcher Jacob Hilton, OpenAI, 2018-23, reinforcement-learning researcher Pamela Mishkin, OpenAI, 2020–26, economics-research team lead Daniel Kokotajlo, OpenAI, 2022–24, governance researcher Alex Turner, Google DeepMind, 2023–26, alignment researcher Jeff Wu, OpenAI, 2018–24, Anthropic, 2024–26, alignment researcher
I’m the editor-in-chief of Asterisk, a Bay Area–based nonprofit magazine that has been covering the AI scene since an LLM passing a high-school math test seemed like a big deal. Asterisk﻿ receives funding from Coefficient Giving, as do some of these sources or their organizations. Some are strangers, and some are friends. They don’t share the same concerns or the same p(doom)s — in fact, they wouldn’t necessarily agree that p(doom) is a coherent concept. But together, they provide a candid view of the AI race and the individual calculus many employees face.
You’re both very concerned about risk from AI and want to motivate the labs to be more careful. Why did you come to believe you would be better able to promote this outcome on the outside? Daniel Kokotajlo: I left OpenAI mostly because I lost confidence that the company, and leadership in particular, would behave responsibly. I wanted more freedom to speak about what I saw coming. I wanted to put on the public record why I had quit.
You could try to do the inside game or you could try to do the outside game, and it seemed to me the inside game was not going to work. Leadership was very adept at listening very carefully to everybody’s things, saying they agreed with them, and then not actually doing anything. And also the culture at the company was biased in favor of overoptimism and self-serving narratives about what they were doing. I really don’t think companies can be trusted to regulate themselves. I’ve had much more impact on the outside, speaking publicly and publishing research, than I would have if I had stayed inside and written more memos.
Jacob Coxon : My thinking was pretty similar to Daniel’s — except it’s closer to crunch time now. It was more from speaking directly to Anthropic leadership about their plans for next year, and I was like, Wow, I don’t want to be part of these plans. It was like, Step one, I don’t want to be part of this. Step two, resign. Step three, tell people, I guess. Step four — I have no idea.
What kinds of plans were they? JC: This was talking directly to people running research. Not Dario Amodei but people who have been at the company for a long time and have a lot of context about the company’s trajectory. They’ve been pretty consistent that 2027 is when things get crazy. The main thing that came up informally in conversation was that people didn’t expect government regulation to happen in time and, in particular, did not expect any sort of international cooperation to be possible. Which maybe shouldn’t have been surprising to me, but it was surprising. I think I’ve always had this expectation that when artificial superintelligence is right around the corner, people will just start taking it seriously and it stops being this fun thing that’s done by labs.
Jacob, you were already concerned about existential risk. To what extent was your mind changed by the things you observed in the past few months at Anthropic, or was this always the trajectory you expected? JC: For me, there’s quite a distinction between my rational beliefs and the things I feel in my gut. If you’d asked me to narrate my opinions when entering Anthropic and when leaving Anthropic, they would probably sound pretty similar. But in terms of the actual feeling between the start and the end, it just felt very, very different.
When I first started, my work did not feel any different from any other form of mathematical research. I knew in the back of my mind that this is the most important industry — that’s why I was working in it. But it didn’t feel important for me to engage with the philosophical questions around it or the details of strategy. That was all other people’s jobs. And then by the end, I’m looking at the projected capabilities of the next round of models we’re going to train, and I just have a gut-level Wow, I am potentially quite scared of the model we’re going to train. And if not this one, then definitely the one afterward.
Can you try to explain to a non-researcher what kinds of things you were noticing? JC: Right now, when we use AIs, the researchers have to provide ideas and direction, and still actually do quite a lot of babysitting. I think there’s a strong possibility that the model generation after the next one will be equally good at coming up with ideas of its own accord. Which means that in the whole research process, rather than a researcher being necessary to provide interesting ideas to the AI, the researcher could literally just say to the AI, “Okay, do good research,” and then let it run. So just very concretely, looking at the capabilities we’re on track to create makes me feel quite viscerally scared and also quite disempowered.
Before you left, whom did you talk to as you were making the decision? JC: I spoke to Daniel because part of leaving was seeing his “ AI 2040” scenario — comparing Plan A to the default trajectory was actually a relatively important thing in internalizing how bad the current trajectory felt. And I spoke to many, many people at Anthropic who had advice about how to leave. Internally, I spoke to people like Holden Karnofsky, and Nick Joseph, head of pretraining, to see what they thought.

articles.title_orig: Then and Now: World War I cenotaph
articles.title_zh: Then and Now: World War I cenotaph
articles.content_orig:
The 13th celebration of Armistice Day in Spokane is remembered for some monumental events.
Although it was a Tuesday, almost all businesses in downtown Spokane closed in honor of the day’s schedule. Most notable was the 12:30 p.m. unveiling of the 12-foot bronze statue of President Abraham Lincoln on a pedestal at Main Avenue and Monroe Street, surrounded by thousands who had just watched the Armistice Day parade. Among the attendees was one of the last Civil War veterans of the region.
But earlier that same day, Spokane’s American Legion Post 9 dedicated a solemn stone cenotaph at Riverside Cemetery, now called Riverside Memorial Park. The 19-by-26-foot platform, made from granite quarried in the Dishman area, consisted of a speaker’s rostrum surrounded by a wall lined with benches and an 8-foot arched stone with the inscription: “In Memory of Those Who Gave Their Lives for their Country in the World War.”
Legion member and architect Henry Bertelsen designed the monument and stonecutter Julian Mosfelt Simonson, also a member, carved the stone. As is typical with a cenotaph, meaning “empty tomb,” no names are inscribed there.
During the war from 1914-18, 11,000 Spokane men served in the military, more than 4,000 went to Europe and almost 200 men from Spokane died in the war.
Almost 500 people attended the dedication, where tearful Gold Star mothers took seats on the cold stone benches surrounding the platform while veterans and families gathered around.
The American Legion was founded in 1919 by the weary veterans of the war in Europe. From its inception, the Legion endeavored to honor past military service, including those from the Civil War and the Spanish -American War. The group would also advocate for veterans benefits and  comfort the bereaved.
Both built in 1920, the Argonne Road bridge and Marne Bridge over Latah Creek were dedicated to returning war veterans, but Legion members wanted to do more. The veterans sold poppies and held other fundraisers to raise the $7,500 to build the memorial, which would be situated near veterans’ burial areas so the platform could be used for future burials.
Some 20 years after the 1930 dedication, an “S” was added to the inscription, changing “World War” to “Wars.”

articles.title_orig: How Congo’s Ebola Epidemic Got So Bad So Quickly
articles.title_zh: How Congo’s Ebola Epidemic Got So Bad So Quickly
articles.content_orig:
Bunia, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history .
More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease, the Reuters news agency notes.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15 , caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine .
Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak, to demand payment for owed wages. They were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
Front-line workers have gone on several strikes since the start of the outbreak to demand payment, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
"The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

A global news roundup, compiled by the Monitor’s international team
Russia facing a growing threat from bears A combination of rising bear numbers and shrinking natural food sources in the forests has led to an unprecedented wave of dangerous encounters in Russia this past summer between bears and people, including several human fatalities. Russia’s bear population has more than doubled to over 300,000 in about three decades, leading authorities to urgently seek new authority to curtail the bear surge, according to the independent news outlet Meduza. – Fred Weir
China supercharges its goal for electric and hybrid cars China has unveiled a bold target for electric and hybrid vehicles – aiming for the vehicles to make up 70% of new passenger vehicle sales by 2030. Such sales are already at 59% for the first eight months of this year. But commercial vehicles are lagging behind, in part because of the lack of charging and refueling networks on long-haul truck routes. The government’s five-year blueprint calls for 40% of new commercial vehicles to be electric or hybrid by 2030, up from 34% now. It also sets stricter targets for fuel efficiency and promotes automated driving, according to the Caixin Global financial news outlet. – Ann Scott Tyson
“We want the police to know that workers are not alone.” That’s what a member of a neighborhood patrol in Buenos Aires told the newspaper El País, describing the rationale for monitoring police operations against street vendors and immigrants. Under Argentina’s President Javier Milei, immigration enforcement has become more visible on the streets. In the capital, a group of neighbors has formed to document arrests of migrants and to protect them from alleged abuse by police. The group was inspired by reports of neighborhood organizing in the United States amid Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations.  – Whitney Eulich
“The illusion of illusions” That’s the title of a research paper by Oxford mathematician Alain Goriely challenging the long-standing theory of optical corrections. The myth goes back 2,000 years and holds that the Parthenon, which sits on the Acropolis overlooking Athens, was intentionally constructed with curves to correct various visual illusions and thus appear straight to the human eye. But the theory “does not withstand close examination,” Professor Goriely writes in the Royal Society Open Science journal after conducting mathematical modeling. “The proposed illusions are either unsupported by evidence or too small to have a perceptible effect under typical viewing conditions.” – Matthew Bell

articles.title_orig: New World screwworm cases climb to 53; new case confirmed in Brewster County dog
articles.title_zh: New World screwworm cases climb to 53; new case confirmed in Brewster County dog
articles.content_orig:
Last updated: Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026 7:00 p.m
There have now been 53 confirmed New World screwworm animal cases in the United States since June, including 51 in Texas and two in New Mexico.
The latest case was confirmed Oct. 2 in a dog in Brewster County, Texas. It is one of three animal cases currently considered active.
The other active cases are goats in Crockett County, Texas, confirmed Sept. 26, and a horse in Grant County, New Mexico, confirmed Sept. 17.
A horse in Presidio County, Texas, confirmed Sept. 9 and previously listed as active, is now considered inactive.
Officials have also recorded one wild screwworm fly detection during the current U.S. outbreak. The fly was found in a surveillance trap in Brewster County on Sept. 25. Fly trap detections are tracked separately and are not included in the 53 animal cases.
Of the 53 animal cases recorded since the first U.S. case was confirmed June 3, 52 have involved domestic animals. No cases have been confirmed in wildlife or feral animals.
Federal officials have said the parasite’s northward spread has slowed, though the threat remains.
The USDA says it has released more than 1 billion sterile flies in Texas since February and is aiming to increase production to 500 million flies a week by next summer.
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins has said officials are making progress in containing the outbreak but have warned that the threat has not passed, particularly in Arizona and New Mexico.
Despite its name, the New World screwworm isn’t a worm. It is the larval stage of the fly (Cochliomyia hominivorax), a parasite that feeds on the living tissue of warm-blooded animals.
Infestations begin when an adult female screwworm fly lays eggs in an open wound or natural body opening. Within hours, the eggs hatch and the larvae begin feeding on living tissue, unlike common maggots, which feed on dead or decaying tissue.
As the larvae burrow deeper into tissue, wounds become larger and often infected. Without treatment, infestations can be fatal.
The screwworm primarily threatens livestock and wildlife, making it a major concern for Texas ranchers and animal health officials.
Human infestations are rare. Most occur when untreated wounds are exposed in areas where the fly is circulating. The current outbreak primarily affects livestock, wildlife and pets.
According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, New World screwworm is not considered a food safety threat. The parasite feeds on living tissue in open wounds — not meat intended for consumers — and animal health and inspection systems are designed to keep infested animals out of the food supply.
Early detection is critical. Animals infected with screwworm may show:
Veterinarians recommend inspecting animals regularly after injuries, surgical procedures, branding or any condition that creates an open wound.
Texas has one of the largest livestock industries in the United States, along with extensive ranchland and abundant wildlife populations, particularly white-tailed deer. That combination makes the state especially vulnerable if screwworm becomes reestablished.
A widespread outbreak could lead to:
The Texas Animal Health Commission and the U.S. Department of Agriculture have expanded surveillance, increased monitoring of animal movement and encouraged rapid reporting of suspected infestations.
The United States eliminated screwworm using one of the most successful pest control programs in history: the sterile insect technique.
Scientists bred and released millions of sterile male flies. Because female screwworm flies typically mate only once, breeding with a sterile male produces no offspring, gradually collapsing the wild population.
That strategy eradicated screwworm from the United States and much of North America. However, the parasite remains present in parts of Central and South America, meaning the risk of reintroduction never fully disappears.
For most Texans, there is no reason to change their daily activities. The greatest risk remains to livestock, pets and wildlife.
Hunters should also inspect harvested game for unusual wounds or signs of infestation and report suspected cases to wildlife officials.
If you suspect an infestation, contact your veterinarian immediately before transporting the animal.
For the latest information and guidance, visit:
The illegal movement of animals — particularly horses — could thwart the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s effort to stop the spread of the parasite.
Texas A&M AgriLife livestock entomologist Sonja Swiger discusses the risks New World screwworm poses to pets, people and livestock, addresses concerns about the food supply and explains why reporting infestations is critical.
Wildlife experts warn that deer may be especially vulnerable because there is no proven way to treat them in the wild.
The New World screwworm has crossed into Texas from Mexico, threatening livestock, wildlife and pets. Human infections are rare, but officials warn the parasite’s spread poses a growing challenge for communities across South Texas.
As the U.S. confronts the return of New World screwworm, researchers at the newly opened Knipling-Bushland U.S. Livestock Insects Research Laboratory in Kerrville are building on the work that helped eradicate the pest decades ago.
The Texas agriculture commissioner supports the move by the federal agency.

articles.title_zh: Microsoft shared Windows 11 26H2 Group Policy templates, settings guidance for admins
articles.content_orig:
Windows powers how people around the world work, learn, create, and connect every day. Today, we’re announcing the availability of the Windows 11 2026 Update, also known as Windows 11, version 26H2. Built on the same servicing foundation as recent Windows 11 releases, version 26H2 delivers the latest Windows innovations with a streamlined update experience designed to minimize disruption and help you stay secure, productive, and up to date.
As organizations and individuals continue to expect faster deployments and less downtime, Windows 11, version 26H2 takes advantage of the same modern servicing technologies that have simplified recent feature updates. For many eligible devices, moving to version 26H2 is as simple as installing a small enablement package, allowing people to start using this new release with minimal download size, quick installation, and a single restart.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is delivered as an enablement package for eligible devices running Windows 11, versions 25H2 and 24H2.
An enablement package is a lightweight update that activates new features already included in the operating system through previous monthly servicing updates. Because versions 26H2, 25H2, and 24H2 share a common servicing branch and underlying codebase, many of the components required for version 26H2 are already present on devices before the feature update becomes available.
This approach enables a significantly faster update experience compared to a traditional operating system upgrade. For eligible devices, installation is similar to a monthly update, requiring only a small download and a quick restart to transition to Windows 11, version 26H2.
As with every Windows release, version 26H2 includes the latest quality, reliability, and security improvements designed to help protect people and organizations while delivering a dependable Windows experience.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is now available for eligible devices running Windows 11, versions 25H2 and 24H2.
To be among the first to receive the update, go to Settings > Windows Update and turn on Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available . Once your device is eligible, you’ll see the option to download and install Windows 11, version 26H2.
As always, we take a measured and data-driven approach to broad availability and will be releasing version 26H2 using a controlled feature rollout. During rollout, we might place safeguard holds on devices where we detect a known compatibility issue that could impact the update experience. We will continue expanding availability over time and provide updates through the Windows release health hub.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is available now through the tools organizations use to manage Windows updates, including Windows Autopatch and the Microsoft 365 admin center [i] .
Existing management tools, update rings, policies, and deployment practices can continue to be used. We recommend that commercial and education customers begin targeted deployments to validate applications, devices, and business-critical workflows before expanding deployment more broadly throughout their organizations.
Windows 11, version 26H2 continues the annual Windows feature update cadence, with a new Windows 11 feature update released during the second half of the calendar year. As with previous annual releases, installing version 26H2 resets the support lifecycle for supported editions of Windows 11. That means 24 months of support for Home and Pro editions and 36 months of support for Enterprise and Education editions.
Select features and enhancements initially released as disabled by default in version 25H2 will be enabled by default in version 26H2. You can find more information on these features, plus guidance to help with planning and deployment, in the Windows IT Pro Blog .
We recommend updating eligible devices to Windows 11, version 26H2 to take advantage of the latest Windows innovations, quality improvements, and security enhancements.
We’ll continue to closely monitor the rollout and share information about known issues, safeguards, and rollout progress through the Windows release health hub and official Windows communications channels.
Thank you for your feedback and partnership as we continue to improve Windows for people and organizations around the world. We love to hear about your experience, so please keep your comments and suggestions coming in via Feedback Hub.
[i] Downloads in the Microsoft 365 admin center and similar channels may be delayed.

articles.title_orig: Pope: May we pray for the intercession of the Virgin Mary for world peace
articles.title_zh: Pope: May we pray for the intercession of the Virgin Mary for world peace
articles.content_orig:
An appeal for wars to end and for peace to be built. The Pope renewed this appeal following the recitation of the Angelus prayer he led from the window of the Apostolic Palace. As he did during his recent visit to Lourdes, France, he again urged everyone to pray the Rosary for peace and unity in the world, standing in solidarity with children who have already begun doing so through the initiative of the Aid to the Church in Need Foundation, âOne Million Children Praying the Holy Rosary.â
âI wholeheartedly thank all the boys and girls who are joining in this prayer in so many parts of the world.  Let us all follow their example, invoking the intercession of the Virgin Mary so that peoples may be freed from the scourge of war.  In particular, let us pray for the Holy Land and for the innocent victims of violence.â
The campaign began at the start of October with the Pope in the Vatican Gardens and will continue until October 7, the Feast of Our Lady of the Rosary. This allows dioceses, parishes, schools, communities, and families on different continents to choose the day that is most suitable for dedicating to this particular intention.
Pope Leo then announced that, on the occasion of the tenth anniversary of Amoris Laetitia, Pope Francisâs post-synodal apostolic exhortation, a week-long gathering will begin next Wednesday, October 7.
It will be held in his presence in the Paul VI Hall, with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Episcopal Conferences, to take stock of the situation of families today. The gathering will include testimonies from bishops and married couples from the five continents.
It will be an opportunity to listen to the voice of the Church at a time of profound change and to find ways to renew and strengthen the choice of marriage, which in various contexts has experienced dramatic declines over the decades. The Pontiff described it this way:
âIt will be a time of synodal discernment for identifying the steps to be taken in order to proclaim the Gospel today among families and the younger generations.  I entrust this task to your prayers and, above all, the families who, with Godâs help, are a sign of hope and an inestimable treasure for the Church and for society.â
The Pope then once again held up Saint Francis as a model, as he had done during the catechesis, on the 800th anniversary of the death of Saint Francis. He expressed his happiness at the many commemorative initiatives, particularly those held in Assisi with the participation of Italyâs highest state authorities. He also offered a special greeting:
âI also greet the amateur radio operators of Assisi and Foligno who spread Saint Francisâ message of peace.â
